course.title: Machine Learning — Zero to Professional
course.subtitle: From your first feature to a production model
course.tagline: A 27-module, ten-section ML school: learn the idea, write the Python, debug it, defend it and ship it.
course.description: This course builds machine learning from the ground up. You start with what learning from data actually means, then Python, NumPy, Pandas, the mathematics and statistics, data preparation, regression, classification, trees and ensembles, evaluation, unsupervised learning, NLP, engineering and deployment. Every module ends with a checkpoint and a defense you can practise. It is designed for a complete beginner who wants entry-level ML Engineer and Data Scientist work, not a vocabulary tour.
outcomes: Explain supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised and reinforcement learning without hand-waving.
Write clean Python, NumPy and Pandas for real tabular data.
Use the mathematics and statistics that models are actually built from.
Run a complete ML workflow: frame, split, train, evaluate, improve and document.
Build regression, classification, tree, ensemble, clustering, anomaly and NLP models.
Choose an evaluation metric that matches the business cost of mistakes.
Prevent data leakage and build reproducible experiments.
Engineer reusable pipelines and deploy a model behind a validated API.
Explain model decisions, limitations, fairness and privacy risks.
Defend a capstone project in an interview-style conversation.

modules.title: Introduction to Machine Learning
modules.goal: Understand what learning from data means, where ML helps, and the vocabulary every later module uses.

topics.title: What is machine learning?
topics.body: Machine learning is a way to write programs that improve at a task by finding patterns in examples instead of being given every rule by hand. The program is the model; the examples are the data; the answer it produces is the prediction. A model is not magic: it is a mathematical rule whose numbers are fitted from data.
topics.code:

total = 10
print(correct / total)

topics.title: A first learning loop
topics.body: A tiny model can already make predictions. Here the model has learned (or been given) slope 2 and intercept 1, and predicts an output for each input. Real training finds those two numbers from data by minimising error; the prediction step looks exactly like this.
topics.code:
samples = [(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7)]
slope = 2
intercept = 1
print([slope * x + intercept for x, _ in samples])

topics.title: Types of machine learning
topics.body: Supervised learning learns from labelled examples (features plus the right answer). Unsupervised learning looks for structure without labels, such as clusters. Semi-supervised learning uses a few labels and many unlabelled examples. Reinforcement learning learns a policy by acting and receiving rewards. Classification predicts a category; regression predicts a number.

interview.q: When should you not use machine learning?
interview.answer: Do not use ML when a deterministic rule is cheaper, auditable and complete; when the data is too small, biased or unavailable; when a single wrong prediction is catastrophic and cannot be reviewed; or when the problem has no learnable pattern. Start with the simplest rule or baseline, and add ML only when measured value justifies its cost and risk.

interview.q: What is the difference between a model parameter and a hyperparameter?
interview.answer: A parameter is learned from the training data, such as a regression weight or a neural-network weight. A hyperparameter is chosen before training, such as a learning rate, tree depth or K in KNN; it controls the learning process and is selected with validation data, never fitted by the training loop itself.

defense.q: Why is a baseline required before a complex model?
defense.answer: A baseline turns "the model looks good" into a measurable claim. A majority-class or simple-rule baseline is cheap, exposes class imbalance, and gives the complex model a number it must beat on the same split and metric.

Grouping customers without labels
Learning a game by reward alone
checkpoint.answer: Predicting house price from labelled sales

checkpoint.q: A model gets 99% accuracy on a fraud dataset with 1% fraud. What should you check?

Only training accuracy

checkpoint.answer: Precision and recall on the fraud class

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning, and name one concrete task for each.
checkpoint.answer: Supervised learning trains on labelled examples to predict a target, such as predicting house price from features. False

checkpoint.solution:

checkpoint.why: The denominator is the full number of validation rows, so 18 / 24 gives 0.75.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why a majority-class baseline is required before evaluating a churn model.
checkpoint.answer: A majority-class baseline predicts the most common label for every row and establishes the score that a real model must beat. It exposes class imbalance: with 10% churn, a constant “no churn” prediction is 90% accurate while catching no churners. Comparing the model with that baseline on the same split and metric prevents a high but meaningless accuracy number from being presented as progress.
rubric: Defines the baseline as always predicting the majority class.
Explains that it exposes imbalance and gives a comparison point.
Requires the same split and metric for a fair comparison.
checkpoint.why: A model is only useful relative to a trivial predictor; without the baseline, accuracy can hide a completely useless classifier.

logic.q: A dataset has 95 negative and 5 positive rows. A model predicts negative for every row. What accuracy does it report, and what does that number hide?
logic.answer: It reports 95% accuracy because 95 of 100 rows are negative. It catches zero positives, so recall on the positive class is 0; accuracy alone hides the complete failure on the class that usually matters most.

learn.title: supervised learning: the working definition
learn.body: supervised learning means learning a mapping from labelled features to a target. In Introduction to Machine Learning, the practical test is whether that definition changes a decision rather than merely appearing in a notebook. Example: predicting a house price from labelled sales records.
learn.realWorld: predicting a house price from labelled sales records

learn.title: supervised learning: why it changes decisions
learn.body: A team can produce a polished model and still get supervised learning wrong. The failure looks like this: treating an unlabelled clustering task as if it had an answer key. The countermeasure is to confirm every training row has a trustworthy target and that the target exists at prediction time and to name the evidence in the design review.
learn.realWorld: confirm every training row has a trustworthy target and that the target exists at prediction time

scores = [77, 84, 91]
weights = [3, 5, 2]

print(f"{rounded:.2f}")
coding.hint: Multiply each score by its weight, sum, then divide by the sum of weights.

logic.q: A dataset has 95 negative and 5 positive rows. A model predicts negative for every row. What accuracy does it report, and what does that number hide?

miniProject.title: Study hours → pass prediction

defense.q: Why is a baseline required before a complex model?
defense.answer: A baseline turns "the model looks good" into a measurable claim. A majority-class or simple-rule baseline is cheap, exposes class imbalance, and gives the complex model a number it must beat on the same split and metric.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (fill in the blank): restore the missing token in this What is machine learning? sample.
checkpoint.code:
correct = ___
total = 10
print(correct / total)
checkpoint.solution:
correct = 8
total = 10
print(correct / total)
checkpoint.why: The missing token is 8; with it restored the sample prints 0.8. Machine learning is a way to write programs that improve at a task by finding patterns in examples instead of being given every rule by hand. The program is the model; the examples are the data; the answer it produces is the prediction. A model is not magic: it is a mathematical rule whose numbers are fitted from data.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (code output): predict exactly what this A first learning loop sample prints.
checkpoint.code:
samples = [(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7)]
slope = 2
intercept = 1
print([slope * x + intercept for x, _ in samples])
checkpoint.why: The verified output is [3, 5, 7]. A tiny model can already make predictions. Here the model has learned (or been given) slope 2 and intercept 1, and predicts an output for each input. Real training finds those two numbers from data by minimising error; the prediction step looks exactly like this.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning, and name one concrete task for each.
checkpoint.answer: Supervised learning trains on labelled examples to predict a target, such as predicting house price from features. Unsupervised learning looks for structure without a target label, such as grouping customers by purchasing behaviour. Both use data, but only supervised learning has an answer key during training.
checkpoint.why: The decisive difference is the presence of a target label; the tasks show that both settings still learn structure from data.
rubric: Names labelled versus unlabelled data, not just “two types of learning”.
Gives one supervised task with a target and one unsupervised task without a target.
States that unsupervised learning still has an objective, even without labels.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (true/false): a model with 99% training accuracy and 70% validation accuracy is probably overfitting.
checkpoint.answer: True
options: True
False
checkpoint.why: The large gap means the model fits training-specific detail that does not transfer. Check for leakage, then simplify or regularise before trusting the training score.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (fill in the blank): restore the denominator in this validation-accuracy calculation.
checkpoint.answer: total
checkpoint.code:
correct = 18
total = 24
print(round(correct / ___, 2))
checkpoint.solution:
correct = 18
total = 24
print(round(correct / total, 2))
checkpoint.why: The denominator is the full number of validation rows, so 18 / 24 gives 0.75.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why a majority-class baseline is required before evaluating a churn model.
checkpoint.answer: A majority-class baseline predicts the most common label for every row and establishes the score that a real model must beat. It exposes class imbalance: with 10% churn, a constant “no churn” prediction is 90% accurate while catching no churners. Comparing the model with that baseline on the same split and metric prevents a high but meaningless accuracy number from being presented as progress.
checkpoint.why: A model is only useful relative to a trivial predictor; without the baseline, accuracy can hide a completely useless classifier.
rubric: Defines the baseline as always predicting the majority class.
Explains that it exposes imbalance and gives a comparison point.
Requires the same split and metric for a fair comparison.

topics.body: A virtual environment isolates the packages for one project. Create it once, activate it, install exact versions with pip, and record them in requirements.txt. Isolation prevents a course experiment from breaking another project, and pinned versions make an experiment reproducible.

interview.q: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
interview.answer: A list is mutable and normally holds a homogeneous sequence you will change. A tuple is immutable, can be hashed if its contents are hashable, and is useful for fixed records, multiple return values and dictionary keys. Immutability is a correctness tool, not just a speed choice.

interview.q: Why is a mutable default argument dangerous in Python?
interview.answer: The default object is created once when the function is defined, not once per call. A list or dictionary default is therefore shared across calls, so appending in one call changes what the next caller sees. Use `None` as the sentinel and create the container inside the function.

scores = [94, 51, 58]
weights = [5, 2, 4]

coding.hint: Multiply each score by its weight, sum, then divide by the sum of weights.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why a mutable default argument can leak state between calls, and state the safe fix.
checkpoint.answer: Python creates the default list or dictionary once when the function is defined, so every call shares the same object. Mutating it in one call changes the value seen by later calls. Use `None` as the default and create a fresh container inside the function.
checkpoint.why: The danger is shared mutable state, not the list syntax; `None` makes the fresh allocation explicit.

modules.title: NumPy for Machine Learning
modules.goal: Use ndarrays, vectorised arithmetic, broadcasting, aggregation and linear algebra as the numerical language of ML.

topics.title: Arrays and vectorisation
topics.body: A NumPy array stores numbers in one compact block and applies operations to all elements without a Python loop. Vectorisation is both shorter and faster; it is how feature matrices and model maths are expressed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a * 2)

topics.title: Aggregation along an axis
topics.body: An axis is the direction you reduce. `axis=0` collapses rows and leaves one value per column; `axis=1` collapses columns and leaves one value per row. Reading the axis correctly prevents most shape bugs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.sum(axis=0))

topics.title: Broadcasting and linear algebra
topics.body: Broadcasting lets arrays with compatible trailing shapes combine without copying, such as subtracting one mean per column from every row. A matrix product is a sum of products, written `X @ w`; it is the core of linear regression, neural layers and PCA.

interview.q: What is the difference between a NumPy view and a copy?
interview.answer: A view shares the original data buffer; changing it can change the base array. A copy owns new memory. Slicing usually returns a view, while boolean indexing and `.copy()` return a copy. Use `.copy()` when you need independent data, and know which one your preprocessing step produced.

interview.q: What does NumPy broadcasting do when arrays of shape (3, 1) and (1, 4) meet?
interview.answer: It aligns the trailing dimensions and stretches each singleton dimension logically, producing a (3, 4) result without physically copying either input. Broadcasting is a shape rule, so the dimensions must be compatible: equal, or one of them must be 1.

coding.title: Vectorised mean squared error
coding.statement: Compute the mean squared error between actual [3, 5, 7] and predicted [2, 5, 8], rounded to two decimals.
coding.starter:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([3, 5, 7])
p = np.array([2, 5, 8])
# print mse
coding.solution:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([3, 5, 7])
p = np.array([2, 5, 8])
print(round(float(np.mean((y - p) ** 2)), 2))
coding.hint: Square the differences first, then take the mean.

coding.title: Column means of a matrix
coding.statement: For the matrix [[1, 2], [3, 4]], print the mean of each column with NumPy.
coding.starter:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
# print column means
coding.solution:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.mean(axis=0))
coding.hint: Reducing down the rows leaves one mean per column.

defense.q: Why does `axis` matter when computing feature means?
defense.answer: A feature mean must be computed per column across rows, which is `axis=0`. Using `axis=1` computes one mean per row and silently produces the wrong shape for later subtraction. Assert shapes before and after; a correct number with the wrong axis is still a bug.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain what `axis=0` does in a NumPy aggregation, and give an example shape change.
checkpoint.answer: `axis=0` collapses the rows, so each output value aggregates down a column. For a `(4, 3)` array, `.sum(axis=0)` returns shape `(3,)`: one sum for each of the three columns. `axis=1` would collapse the columns and return `(4,)`.

checkpoint.answer: An axis is the dimension being reduced. For a (4, 3) array, `.sum(axis=0)` collapses the rows and returns shape (3,), one total per column; `.sum(axis=1)` collapses the columns and returns shape (4,), one total per row. Reading the axis correctly prevents plausible but transposed results.
rubric: Defines the axis as the dimension being reduced.

checkpoint.why: A correct number on the wrong axis can still be a bug; the shape makes the intended reduction explicit.

logic.q: For a NumPy array of shape (4, 3), what shape does `.mean(axis=1)` return, and what does each value mean?
logic.answer: It returns shape (4,), one value per row. `axis=1` collapses the three columns of each row, so each result is the mean of that row.

learn.realWorld: a basic slice whose mutation changes the base array

learn.title: view: why it changes decisions
learn.body: A team can produce a polished model and still get view wrong. The failure looks like this: editing a view and being surprised that the source changed. The countermeasure is to use .copy() when independence is required and test the base array afterwards and to name the evidence in the design review.
learn.realWorld: use .copy() when independence is required and test the base array afterwards

learn.title: view: the failure mode
learn.body: The common failure is that editing a view and being surprised that the source changed. That can survive a green dashboard because the aggregate looks healthy. Check it by asking whether you can use .copy() when independence is required and test the base array afterwards before the model reaches a user.

learn.title: view: how to verify it

learn.title: view vs matrix product
learn.body: view means an array that shares the original data buffer. matrix product means a sum of products between rows of one matrix and columns of another. They are easy to conflate, but confusing them changes which evidence a reviewer should ask for.

interview.q: What is the difference between a NumPy view and a copy?
interview.answer: A view shares the original data buffer; changing it can change the base array. A copy owns new memory. Slicing usually returns a view, while boolean indexing and `.copy()` return a copy. Use `.copy()` when you need independent data, and know which one your preprocessing step produced.

interview.q: What does NumPy broadcasting do when arrays of shape (3, 1) and (1, 4) meet?
interview.answer: It aligns the trailing dimensions and stretches each singleton dimension logically, producing a (3, 4) result without physically copying either input. Broadcasting is a shape rule, so the dimensions must be compatible: equal, or one of them must be 1.

coding.title: Vectorised mean squared error
coding.statement: Compute the mean squared error between actual [3, 5, 7] and predicted [2, 5, 8], rounded to two decimals.
coding.starter:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([3, 5, 7])
p = np.array([2, 5, 8])
# print mse
coding.solution:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([3, 5, 7])
p = np.array([2, 5, 8])
print(round(float(np.mean((y - p) ** 2)), 2))
coding.hint: Square the differences first, then take the mean.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Arrays and vectorisation

import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a * 2)

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Aggregation along an axis
practice.task: An axis is the direction you reduce. `axis=0` collapses rows and leaves one value per column; `axis=1` collapses columns and leaves one value per row. Reading the axis correctly prevents most shape bugs.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.sum(axis=0))

defense.q: Why does `axis` matter when computing feature means?
defense.answer: A feature mean must be computed per column across rows, which is `axis=0`. Using `axis=1` computes one mean per row and silently produces the wrong shape for later subtraction. Assert shapes before and after; a correct number with the wrong axis is still a bug.

defense.q: NumPy for Machine Learning · Defend your approach to ndarray in a design review for NumPy for Machine Learning.
defense.answer: We treat ndarray as a compact, typed, fixed-shape block of numeric data. The evidence is that we can assert dtype and shape before arithmetic or indexing. The limitation is that assuming a list operation and an array operation have the same semantics

defense.q: NumPy for Machine Learning · An interviewer challenges you: “assuming a list operation and an array operation have the same semantics” How do you respond?
defense.answer: I would not defend the claim without evidence. I would show whether we can assert dtype and shape before arithmetic or indexing, and if we cannot, I would treat ndarray as an open risk rather than a solved property.

defense.q: NumPy for Machine Learning · A production review asks for evidence on ndarray. What do you show?

modules.title: Pandas for Machine Learning
modules.goal: Load, inspect, filter, group, join and clean tabular data without losing track of rows or types.

topics.title: Series, DataFrames and groupby
topics.body: A Series is one labelled column; a DataFrame is a table of aligned Series. `groupby` splits rows by a key, applies an aggregation and combines the result, which is the fastest way to turn raw transactions into features.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi", "Pune"], "marks": [80, 90, 70]})
print(df.groupby("city")["marks"].mean()["Pune"])

topics.title: Finding missing values
topics.body: Missing data is a fact to measure, not an error to hide. `isna().sum()` reports how many values are absent per column; that count decides whether to drop, impute or investigate the collection process.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, None, 30])
print(int(s.isna().sum()))

topics.title: Merging, selection and safe assignment
topics.body: Use `merge` for key-based joins, `loc` for label-based selection and `iloc` for position-based selection. Prefer one explicit assignment such as `df.loc[mask, "col"] = value` over chained indexing, which can silently operate on a copy. Always check row counts before and after a join.

interview.q: What is the difference between `.loc` and `.iloc`?
interview.answer: `.loc` selects by index/column labels and supports boolean masks. `.iloc` selects by integer position, like normal Python indexing. Mixing them causes confusing errors, especially with a non-default index; choose based on whether you mean a name or a position.

interview.q: What does Pandas `groupby` actually do internally?
interview.answer: It splits the rows by key, applies the requested aggregation or transformation to each group, and combines the results into a new Series or DataFrame. Group keys that are missing are excluded by default, which is why a null category can silently disappear from a report.

coding.title: Revenue for one product
coding.statement: Given a product/revenue DataFrame, print the total revenue for product A as an integer.
coding.starter:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"product": ["A", "B", "A"], "revenue": [10, 20, 15]})
# print A total
coding.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"product": ["A", "B", "A"], "revenue": [10, 20, 15]})
print(int(df.groupby("product")["revenue"].sum()["A"]))
coding.hint: Group first, then select A.

coding.title: Count missing cells
coding.statement: For a DataFrame with two columns, count every missing cell in the whole table and print the integer total.
coding.starter:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3], "b": [None, 5, None]})
# print total missing cells
coding.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3], "b": [None, 5, None]})
print(int(df.isna().sum().sum()))
coding.hint: Sum the boolean mask once for each axis.

debug.title: Forgetting to call the aggregation
debug.broken:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [40, 60, 80]})
print(df["marks"].mean)
debug.error: This prints a bound method object, not 60.0. `mean` is a method; call it with parentheses.
debug.fix:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [40, 60, 80]})
print(df["marks"].mean())

defense.q: Why is chained assignment dangerous in Pandas?
defense.answer: Chained indexing can return a temporary copy, so the assignment may not modify the original DataFrame. Pandas also warns about it. Use a single `.loc[row_mask, column]` assignment, and verify the affected row count.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain the difference between `.loc` and `.iloc`, and state which is safer after a sort.
checkpoint.answer: `.loc` selects by index label, while `.iloc` selects by integer position. After sorting or filtering, positions change but labels still identify the original rows, so `.loc` is safer when the label is the intended key. `.iloc` is appropriate when the question is literally “the first three rows”.

checkpoint.why: The common bug is using `.iloc` after a sort and silently selecting a different row; the label is the stable identity.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why chained assignment in Pandas can silently fail to update the original DataFrame.
checkpoint.answer: Chained indexing such as `df[df.a > 0]["b"] = 1` can operate on a temporary copy, so the assignment may not reach the original object. Pandas may also emit a SettingWithCopy warning. Use one explicit `.loc[row_mask, "b"] = 1` assignment and verify the number of changed rows.
rubric: Explains the temporary-copy or uncertain-target problem.
Contrasts chained indexing with a single `.loc` assignment.
Requires checking the affected rows after the assignment.
checkpoint.why: The bug is dangerous because the code may run without an exception while leaving the source unchanged.

logic.q: A DataFrame has five rows. Its right table has unique keys and exactly two left rows match. How many rows does an inner merge return?
logic.answer: Two rows. An inner merge keeps only matching keys, and because the right keys are unique each matching left row produces one row.

interview.q: What is the difference between `.loc` and `.iloc`?
interview.answer: `.loc` selects by index/column labels and supports boolean masks. `.iloc` selects by integer position, like normal Python indexing. Mixing them causes confusing errors, especially with a non-default index; choose based on whether you mean a name or a position.

interview.q: What does Pandas `groupby` actually do internally?
interview.answer: It splits the rows by key, applies the requested aggregation or transformation to each group, and combines the results into a new Series or DataFrame. Group keys that are missing are excluded by default, which is why a null category can silently disappear from a report.

coding.title: Revenue for one product
coding.statement: Given a product/revenue DataFrame, print the total revenue for product A as an integer.
coding.starter:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"product": ["A", "B", "A"], "revenue": [10, 20, 15]})
# print A total
coding.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"product": ["A", "B", "A"], "revenue": [10, 20, 15]})
print(int(df.groupby("product")["revenue"].sum()["A"]))
coding.hint: Group first, then select A.

coding.title: Count missing cells
coding.statement: For a DataFrame with two columns, count every missing cell in the whole table and print the integer total.
coding.starter:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3], "b": [None, 5, None]})
# print total missing cells
coding.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3], "b": [None, 5, None]})
print(int(df.isna().sum().sum()))
coding.hint: Sum the boolean mask once for each axis.

scores = [78, 85, 92]
weights = [4, 1, 3]

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Series, DataFrames and groupby
practice.task: A Series is one labelled column; a DataFrame is a table of aligned Series. `groupby` splits rows by a key, applies an aggregation and combines the result, which is the fastest way to turn raw transactions into features.
practice.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi", "Pune"], "marks": [80, 90, 70]})
print(df.groupby("city")["marks"].mean()["Pune"])

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Finding missing values
practice.task: Missing data is a fact to measure, not an error to hide. `isna().sum()` reports how many values are absent per column; that count decides whether to drop, impute or investigate the collection process.

s = pd.Series([10, None, 30])
print(int(s.isna().sum()))

defense.q: Why is chained assignment dangerous in Pandas?
defense.answer: Chained indexing can return a temporary copy, so the assignment may not modify the original DataFrame. Pandas also warns about it. Use a single `.loc[row_mask, column]` assignment, and verify the affected row count.

defense.q: Pandas for Machine Learning · Defend your approach to Series in a design review for Pandas for Machine Learning.
defense.answer: We treat Series as a labelled one-dimensional array. The evidence is that we can inspect index, dtype and length before and after every transformation. The limitation is that treating the index as if it were a normal integer position after a filter

defense.q: Pandas for Machine Learning · An interviewer challenges you: “treating the index as if it were a normal integer position after a filter” How do you respond?

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain the difference between `.loc` and `.iloc`, and state which is safer after a sort.
checkpoint.answer: `.loc` selects by index label, while `.iloc` selects by integer position. checkpoint.why: The common bug is using `.iloc` after a sort and silently selecting a different row; the label is the stable identity.

modules.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
modules.goal: Build the vectors, matrices, derivatives, gradients and optimisation intuition behind model training.

topics.title: Vectors, dot products and predictions
topics.body: A feature row and a weight vector are both vectors. Their dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them, producing one prediction. This one operation underlies linear regression, logistic regression and every neural-network layer.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
w = np.array([2.0, -1.0])
x = np.array([3.0, 4.0])
print(float(w @ x))

topics.title: A gradient descent step
topics.body: A gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. To reduce a loss, move the parameter in the opposite direction, scaled by a learning rate. One step is `w_new = w - learning_rate * gradient`.
topics.code:
w = 4.0
gradient = 8.0
learning_rate = 0.1
print(round(w - learning_rate * gradient, 2))

topics.title: Derivatives, chain rule and loss
topics.body: A derivative measures how a tiny change in an input changes an output. The chain rule composes those rates through nested operations, which is exactly what backpropagation does. A loss function turns "how wrong" into a number that optimisation can reduce; mean squared error and log loss are two common choices.

interview.q: Why do we subtract the gradient instead of adding it?
interview.answer: The gradient points toward increasing loss. Training wants lower loss, so we step in the negative-gradient direction. The learning rate controls the step size; too large can overshoot, too small is slow.

interview.q: What is the difference between a derivative and a gradient?

coding.title: One gradient descent update
coding.statement: Start with w = 2.0, gradient = 6.0 and learning rate 0.5. Print the updated w.
coding.starter:
w = 2.0
gradient = 6.0
lr = 0.5
# update
coding.solution:
w = 2.0
gradient = 6.0
lr = 0.5
w = w - lr * gradient
print(w)
coding.hint: Move opposite to the gradient.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why gradient descent subtracts the learning rate times the gradient.
checkpoint.answer: The gradient points toward the steepest increase of the loss. To reduce the loss, we move in the opposite direction, so the update is parameter minus learning rate times gradient. The learning rate controls the step size: too large can overshoot, too small is slow.
checkpoint.why: The sign is the core: adding the gradient ascends, subtracting descends; the learning rate only scales the step.

modules.title: Probability and Statistics
modules.goal: Describe uncertainty, compare groups and interpret evidence instead of trusting a single average.

topics.title: Mean and standard deviation
topics.body: The mean is the balance point of a distribution; standard deviation describes typical distance from it. Together they summarise centre and spread, and they are the basis of standardisation and z-scores.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
xs = np.array([2, 4, 6])
print(float(np.mean(xs)), round(float(np.std(xs)), 2))

topics.title: Bayes theorem in one calculation
topics.body: Bayes updates a prior belief with evidence. The posterior is prior × likelihood ÷ evidence. It is the foundation of Naive Bayes and of reasoning about false positives in medical or fraud screening.
topics.code:
prior = 0.1
likelihood = 0.8
evidence = 0.2
print(round(prior * likelihood / evidence, 2))

topics.title: Sampling, intervals and hypothesis tests
topics.body: A sample statistic varies from sample to sample. A confidence interval expresses that uncertainty, while a hypothesis test asks whether an observed difference is plausible under a null model. A p-value is not the probability that the null is true, and statistical significance is not business importance.

interview.q: What does a p-value actually mean?
interview.answer: It is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as ours, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, nor the probability of replication. Report an effect size and interval alongside it.

interview.q: What is the difference between standard deviation and standard error?
interview.answer: Standard deviation describes the spread of individual observations around the mean. Standard error describes the uncertainty of an estimated statistic, commonly the mean, and shrinks roughly as 1/√n as the sample grows.

coding.title: A Bayes update
coding.statement: A prior of 0.2 and likelihood of 0.5 meet evidence 0.25. Print the posterior rounded to two decimals.
coding.starter:
prior = 0.2
likelihood = 0.5
evidence = 0.25
# posterior
coding.solution:
prior = 0.2
likelihood = 0.5
evidence = 0.25
print(round(prior * likelihood / evidence, 2))
coding.hint: Multiply prior by likelihood, then divide by evidence.

coding.title: Standard error of the mean
coding.statement: For [2, 4, 6], print the sample standard error of the mean, rounded to three decimals.
coding.starter:
import math
import statistics
xs = [2, 4, 6]
# print the standard error
coding.solution:
import math
import statistics
xs = [2, 4, 6]
print(round(statistics.stdev(xs) / math.sqrt(len(xs)), 3))
coding.hint: Sample standard deviation divided by the square root of n.

debug.title: Adding a constant to Bayes
debug.broken:
prior = 0.2
likelihood = 0.5
evidence = 0.25
posterior = prior * likelihood / evidence + 0.1
print(round(posterior, 2))
debug.error: The result is 0.5, but the Bayes posterior is 0.4. The extra 0.1 is not part of the formula.
debug.fix:
prior = 0.2
likelihood = 0.5
evidence = 0.25
posterior = prior * likelihood / evidence
print(round(posterior, 2))

defense.q: Why can a statistically significant result be useless in production?
defense.answer: With a large enough sample, a tiny effect becomes statistically significant. Production cares about effect size, cost, latency and user impact. A significant 0.01% lift can be smaller than noise in revenue or more expensive to ship than it returns.
steps: Compare with the cost of change.
Check the interval, not just p.

It is not the probability that the null is true, nor the probability that the result will replicate. checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain what a 95% confidence interval means and what it does not guarantee.
checkpoint.answer: A 95% confidence interval is produced by a procedure that would capture the true parameter in about 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. It expresses uncertainty around an estimate, not the probability that this particular interval contains the truth. It also does not guarantee that the study was unbiased or that the effect is practically important.
rubric: Describes the repeated-sampling or procedure-based meaning.
Avoids claiming a 95% probability for this specific interval.
Mentions assumptions, bias or practical importance as separate issues.
checkpoint.why: The confidence level belongs to the procedure, while a single interval is either covering or not.

logic.q: A disease has 1% prevalence. A test has 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity. If a person tests positive, is the probability of disease close to 90%?
logic.answer: No. It is about 8.3%. With 10,000 people, about 90 true positives and 990 false positives occur; the positive predictive value is 90 / (90 + 990), because the low base rate dominates the false positives.

learn.title: mean: the working definition
learn.body: mean means the arithmetic balance point of a set of values. In Probability and Statistics, the practical test is whether that definition changes a decision rather than merely appearing in a notebook. Example: the average of 2, 4 and 6 is 4.
learn.realWorld: the average of 2, 4 and 6 is 4

learn.title: mean: why it changes decisions
learn.body: A team can produce a polished model and still get mean wrong. The failure looks like this: reporting a mean for a skewed distribution without the median. The countermeasure is to show mean, median, spread and sample size together and to name the evidence in the design review.
learn.realWorld: show mean, median, spread and sample size together

learn.title: mean: a worked example
learn.body: Start with this case: the average of 2, 4 and 6 is 4. Notice that the lesson is not the number alone; mean is the property being checked. A useful review question is: show mean, median, spread and sample size together.
learn.realWorld: the average of 2, 4 and 6 is 4

learn.title: mean: the failure mode
learn.body: The common failure is that reporting a mean for a skewed distribution without the median. That can survive a green dashboard because the aggregate looks healthy. Check it by asking whether you can show mean, median, spread and sample size together before the model reaches a user.
learn.realWorld: reporting a mean for a skewed distribution without the median

learn.title: mean: how to verify it
learn.body: Before shipping, show mean, median, spread and sample size together. Keep the evidence with the model version. If the team cannot show that evidence, mean is an assumption, not a verified property.
learn.realWorld: show mean, median, spread and sample size together

learn.title: mean vs standard deviation
learn.body: mean means the arithmetic balance point of a set of values. standard deviation means a typical distance of observations from their mean. They are easy to conflate, but confusing them changes which evidence a reviewer should ask for.
learn.realWorld: mean: the average of 2, 4 and 6 is 4

learn.title: mean: a design-review answer
learn.body: When asked how the team handles mean, answer with a mechanism and an artifact: show mean, median, spread and sample size together. Then name the limitation: reporting a mean for a skewed distribution without the median. Intent alone is not an answer.
learn.realWorld: show mean, median, spread and sample size together

logic.q: A disease has 1% prevalence. A test has 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity. If a person tests positive, is the probability of disease close to 90%?
logic.answer: No. It is about 8.3%. With 10,000 people, about 90 true positives and 990 false positives occur; the positive predictive value is 90 / (90 + 990), because the low base rate dominates the false positives.

defense.q: Why can a statistically significant result be useless in production?
defense.answer: With a large enough sample, a tiny effect becomes statistically significant. Production cares about effect size, cost, latency and user impact. A significant 0.01% lift can be smaller than noise in revenue or more expensive to ship than it returns.
steps: Compare with the cost of change.
Check the interval, not just p.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain what a p-value does and does not mean.
checkpoint.answer: A p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as ours, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, nor the probability that the result will replicate. A small p-value is evidence against the null under the model, not proof of a large or important effect.
checkpoint.why: The p-value is a tail probability about data under a null; reversing it into “probability the null is true” is the common error.

modules.title: Exploratory Data Analysis
modules.goal: Profile a dataset, see distributions and relationships, and turn a business question into testable features.

topics.title: Measure missingness before cleaning
topics.body: The first EDA question is what is absent. A missing-value count per column reveals collection problems and decides whether dropping rows would bias the sample.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, None, 30])
print(int(s.isna().sum()))

topics.title: Correlation between two numeric columns
topics.body: Correlation summarises the direction and strength of a linear relationship on a -1 to 1 scale. It is a screening tool, not proof of causation, and it can miss non-linear structure.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [2, 4, 6]})
print(round(float(df["x"].corr(df["y"])), 2))

topics.title: Univariate, bivariate and multivariate views
topics.body: Univariate analysis describes one variable at a time (histogram, boxplot, counts). Bivariate analysis compares two (scatter, grouped summary). Multivariate analysis looks at interactions and confounding. Always inspect the target separately, because a feature can look harmless overall and still separate the classes.

interview.q: Why does correlation not imply causation?
interview.answer: Two variables can move together because a third variable drives both, because of selection in the sample, or by coincidence. Establishing causation needs a design such as randomisation or a defensible causal model, not a large correlation coefficient.

interview.q: What is the difference between data missing at random and data missing not at random?
interview.answer: Missing at random means the probability of missingness can be explained by observed variables; a model using those variables can impute it without a special missingness model. Missing not at random means the missing value itself drives whether it is missing, such as high earners refusing to report income; that needs a stronger assumption or a sensitivity analysis.

coding.title: Count IQR outliers
coding.statement: Using the 1.5×IQR rule, count outliers in [10, 12, 11, 100] and print the count.
coding.starter:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 12, 11, 100])
# count outliers
coding.solution:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 12, 11, 100])
q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
print(int((s > q3 + 1.5 * iqr).sum()))
coding.hint: The upper fence is Q3 plus 1.5 times the IQR.

coding.title: Missing percentage
coding.statement: For [1, None, 3, None], print the missing percentage as a number.
coding.starter:
values = [1, None, 3, None]
# print the missing percentage
coding.solution:
values = [1, None, 3, None]
print(sum(value is None for value in values) / len(values) * 100)
coding.hint: Count missing values, divide by the total, then multiply by 100.

debug.title: Calling a numeric method on text
debug.broken:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi"]})
print(df["city"].mean())
debug.error: Pandas raises TypeError because the mean of strings is undefined. The intended analysis is a count or a numeric column, not an average of city names.
debug.fix:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi"]})
print(df["city"].value_counts())

defense.q: Why inspect the target before feature engineering?
defense.answer: The target determines the task, the metric and the split. Looking at its distribution exposes imbalance, outliers and leakage risks early, and prevents building features that are only available after the outcome is known.

checkpoint.q: Which plot is best for one numeric variable’s distribution?

checkpoint.q: A correlation of 0 means:
options: No linear relationship
No relationship of any kind
The variables are identical
checkpoint.answer: No linear relationship
checkpoint.why: A non-linear relationship can still exist.

checkpoint.q: True or false: a correlation of exactly zero proves that two variables are independent.
options: True
False
checkpoint.answer: False
checkpoint.why: Correlation captures linear association only. A strong non-linear relationship can have zero linear correlation while the variables remain dependent.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why correlation does not imply causation, and name one confounder that could explain a positive correlation.
checkpoint.answer: Correlation measures linear association, but two variables can move together because a third variable drives both, or because of reverse causation. For example, ice-cream sales and drowning rates correlate, but hot weather increases both. Causation requires a design or assumption that rules out such confounders.
rubric: Distinguishes association from a causal mechanism.
Names a concrete confounder or a reverse-causation path.
States what additional evidence or design would be needed for a causal claim.
checkpoint.why: A confounder changes both variables, creating a correlation with no direct causal edge; the weather example makes that mechanism concrete.

checkpoint.why: Correlation measures linear association only. A strong non-linear relationship can have zero linear correlation, so inspect the scatter plot.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why missingness should be measured before choosing a cleaning strategy.
checkpoint.answer: Missingness can be concentrated in a subgroup or in the target itself, so dropping rows can silently change the population. Measure missing counts by column, by target class and over time. Then decide whether to drop, impute or investigate the collection process, and document the assumption behind that choice.
rubric: Connects missingness patterns to bias or population change.
Recommends measuring by column and by target or time.
Chooses a strategy with a documented assumption rather than defaulting to drop.
checkpoint.why: The cleaning method is a modelling decision; without the pattern, a convenient fill can distort the signal.

logic.q: A correlation coefficient is exactly 0. Does that prove the two variables are independent?
logic.answer: No. Correlation measures linear association only. Two variables can have a strong non-linear relationship, such as a parabola, while their linear correlation is zero; always inspect the scatter plot before concluding independence.

learn.title: missingness: the working definition
learn.body: missingness means the pattern and amount of absent data in a column or row. In Exploratory Data Analysis, the practical test is whether that definition changes a decision rather than merely appearing in a notebook. Example: income missing for 18% of applicants.
learn.realWorld: income missing for 18% of applicants

learn.title: missingness: why it changes decisions
learn.body: A team can produce a polished model and still get missingness wrong. The failure looks like this: dropping all incomplete rows and silently changing the population. The countermeasure is to report missingness by column, by target class and over time and to name the evidence in the design review.
learn.realWorld: report missingness by column, by target class and over time

learn.title: missingness: a worked example
learn.body: Start with this case: income missing for 18% of applicants. Notice that the lesson is not the number alone; missingness is the property being checked. A useful review question is: report missingness by column, by target class and over time.
learn.realWorld: income missing for 18% of applicants

learn.title: missingness: the failure mode
learn.body: The common failure is that dropping all incomplete rows and silently changing the population. That can survive a green dashboard because the aggregate looks healthy. Check it by asking whether you can report missingness by column, by target class and over time before the model reaches a user.
learn.realWorld: dropping all incomplete rows and silently changing the population

learn.title: missingness: how to verify it
learn.body: Before shipping, report missingness by column, by target class and over time. Keep the evidence with the model version. If the team cannot show that evidence, missingness is an assumption, not a verified property.
learn.realWorld: report missingness by column, by target class and over time

learn.title: missingness vs distribution
learn.body: missingness means the pattern and amount of absent data in a column or row. distribution means the shape, centre, spread and tails of a variable. They are easy to conflate, but confusing them changes which evidence a reviewer should ask for.

interview.q: Why does correlation not imply causation?
interview.answer: Two variables can move together because a third variable drives both, because of selection in the sample, or by coincidence. Establishing causation needs a design such as randomisation or a defensible causal model, not a large correlation coefficient.

interview.q: What is the difference between data missing at random and data missing not at random?
interview.answer: Missing at random means the probability of missingness can be explained by observed variables; a model using those variables can impute it without a special missingness model. Missing not at random means the missing value itself drives whether it is missing, such as high earners refusing to report income; that needs a stronger assumption or a sensitivity analysis.

coding.title: Count IQR outliers
coding.statement: Using the 1.5×IQR rule, count outliers in [10, 12, 11, 100] and print the count.
coding.starter:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 12, 11, 100])
# count outliers
coding.solution:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 12, 11, 100])
q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
print(int((s > q3 + 1.5 * iqr).sum()))
coding.hint: The upper fence is Q3 plus 1.5 times the IQR.

coding.title: ml07 · weighted average · coding drill 1
coding.statement: Exploratory Data Analysis: Scores 79, 86, 93 have weights 5, 2, 4. What is the weighted average, rounded to two decimals? Write a complete Python snippet; the expected output is checked by the course test.
coding.starter:
import math
scores = [79, 86, 93]
weights = [5, 2, 4]
# calculate the requested value and print it to two decimals
coding.solution:
import math
scores = [79, 86, 93]
weights = [5, 2, 4]
answer = sum(score * weight for score, weight in zip(scores, weights)) / sum(weights)
rounded = math.floor(answer * 100 + 0.5) / 100
print(f"{rounded:.2f}")
coding.hint: Multiply each score by its weight, sum, then divide by the sum of weights.

logic.q: A correlation coefficient is exactly 0. Does that prove the two variables are independent?
logic.answer: No. Correlation measures linear association only. Two variables can have a strong non-linear relationship, such as a parabola, while their linear correlation is zero; always inspect the scatter plot before concluding independence.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Correlation between two numeric columns
practice.task: Correlation summarises the direction and strength of a linear relationship on a -1 to 1 scale. It is a screening tool, not proof of causation, and it can miss non-linear structure.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [2, 4, 6]})

defense.q: Why inspect the target before feature engineering?
defense.answer: The target determines the task, the metric and the split. Looking at its distribution exposes imbalance, outliers and leakage risks early, and prevents building features that are only available after the outcome is known.

defense.q: Exploratory Data Analysis · Defend your approach to missingness in a design review for Exploratory Data Analysis.
defense.answer: We treat missingness as the pattern and amount of absent data in a column or row. The evidence is that we can report missingness by column, by target class and over time. The limitation is that dropping all incomplete rows and silently changing the population

defense.q: Exploratory Data Analysis · An interviewer challenges you: “dropping all incomplete rows and silently changing the population” How do you respond?
defense.answer: I would not defend the claim without evidence. I would show whether we can report missingness by column, by target class and over time, and if we cannot, I would treat missingness as an open risk rather than a solved property.

defense.q: Exploratory Data Analysis · A production review asks for evidence on missingness. What do you show?

steps: Tie it to the model version.

defense.q: Exploratory Data Analysis · What is the limitation of missingness, and how do you communicate it?
defense.answer: The limitation is that dropping all incomplete rows and silently changing the population. I would state it in the model card and pair it with the specific check “report missingness by column, by target class and over time” rather than implying the metric proves more than it does.
steps: Put it in the model card.

defense.q: Exploratory Data Analysis · If missingness fails after launch, what is your first response?
defense.answer: First contain the decision or alert path affected by the failure: dropping all incomplete rows and silently changing the population. checkpoint.q: A correlation of 0 means:
checkpoint.answer: No linear relationship
options: No linear relationship
No relationship of any kind
The variables are identical
checkpoint.why: A non-linear relationship can still exist.

checkpoint.q: True or false: a correlation of exactly zero proves that two variables are independent.
checkpoint.answer: False
options: True
False
checkpoint.why: Correlation captures linear association only. A strong non-linear relationship can have zero linear correlation while the variables remain dependent.

import pandas as pd

checkpoint.solution:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, None, 30])
print(int(s.isna().sum()))
checkpoint.why: The missing token is 30; with it restored the sample prints 1. The first EDA question is what is absent. A missing-value count per column reveals collection problems and decides whether dropping rows would bias the sample.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (code output): predict exactly what this Correlation between two numeric columns sample prints.
checkpoint.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [2, 4, 6]})
print(round(float(df["x"].corr(df["y"])), 2))
checkpoint.why: The verified output is 1.0. Correlation summarises the direction and strength of a linear relationship on a -1 to 1 scale. It is a screening tool, not proof of causation, and it can miss non-linear structure.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why correlation does not imply causation, and name one confounder that could explain a positive correlation.
checkpoint.answer: Correlation measures linear association, but two variables can move together because a third variable drives both, or because of reverse causation. For example, ice-cream sales and drowning rates correlate, but hot weather increases both. Causation requires a design or assumption that rules out such confounders.
checkpoint.why: A confounder changes both variables, creating a correlation with no direct causal edge; the weather example makes that mechanism concrete.
rubric: Distinguishes association from a causal mechanism.
Names a concrete confounder or a reverse-causation path.
States what additional evidence or design would be needed for a causal claim.

modules.title: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering
modules.goal: Make features model-ready without leaking future or test information into training.

topics.title: Standardise a numeric feature
topics.body: Standardisation subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, giving a feature with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Fit those statistics on training data only, then apply the same numbers at inference.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
print([round(float(v), 2) for v in (x - x.mean()) / x.std()])

topics.title: One-hot encode a category
topics.body: One-hot encoding creates one binary column per category so a model does not invent an order between labels. Drop one column when a linear model has an intercept to avoid perfect collinearity, and handle unseen categories at inference.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"color": ["red", "blue"]})

topics.title: Data leakage and train/inference consistency
topics.body: Leakage is any information in training that will not be available at prediction time, or any statistic computed using test rows. Examples: scaling before splitting, target-derived features, future dates, and imputing with the full-dataset mean. Build one preprocessing object, fit it on training data, and reuse it unchanged for validation, test and production.

interview.q: Why must an imputer or scaler be fitted on training data only?
interview.answer: Fitting on all rows lets test-set statistics influence training, producing an optimistic estimate that will not reproduce in production. Fit on training data, then transform validation, test and live inputs with the same stored parameters.

interview.q: Why is one-hot encoding usually preferred over integer codes for unordered categories?
interview.answer: Integer codes imply an order and a distance: a model may treat “blue = 2” as twice “red = 1” and can interpolate a category that does not exist. One-hot encoding gives each category its own binary column, removing the false ordering at the cost of more columns.

checkpoint.answer: Fitting computes statistics such as the mean, standard deviation or median. If those statistics include validation or test rows, information from the evaluation data leaks into training and the score becomes optimistic. checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why one-hot encoding is usually preferred to integer codes for unordered categories.
checkpoint.answer: Integer codes imply an order and a distance that the categories do not have; a model can treat “blue = 2” as twice “red = 1”. One-hot encoding gives each category its own binary column, removing the false ordering. It costs more columns and needs an explicit strategy for unseen categories.

logic.q: A one-hot encoder was fitted on red and green, then sees blue at inference. What should happen?
logic.answer: It should not silently map blue to red or green. A safe encoder is configured to ignore unknown categories, producing all zeros, or to reserve an explicit “unknown” column; the choice must match how the model was trained and be documented.

learn.title: standardisation: the working definition
learn.body: standardisation means subtracting the training mean and dividing by the training standard deviation. In Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering, the practical test is whether that definition changes a decision rather than merely appearing in a notebook. Example: converting features with different units into comparable z-scores.
learn.realWorld: converting features with different units into comparable z-scores

learn.title: standardisation: why it changes decisions
learn.body: A team can produce a polished model and still get standardisation wrong. The failure looks like this: fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting. The countermeasure is to fit on training rows only and reuse the stored statistics at inference and to name the evidence in the design review.
learn.realWorld: fit on training rows only and reuse the stored statistics at inference

learn.title: standardisation: a worked example
learn.body: Start with this case: converting features with different units into comparable z-scores. Notice that the lesson is not the number alone; standardisation is the property being checked. A useful review question is: fit on training rows only and reuse the stored statistics at inference.
learn.realWorld: converting features with different units into comparable z-scores

learn.title: standardisation: the failure mode
learn.body: The common failure is that fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting. That can survive a green dashboard because the aggregate looks healthy. Check it by asking whether you can fit on training rows only and reuse the stored statistics at inference before the model reaches a user.
learn.realWorld: fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting

learn.title: standardisation: how to verify it
learn.body: Before shipping, fit on training rows only and reuse the stored statistics at inference. Keep the evidence with the model version. If the team cannot show that evidence, standardisation is an assumption, not a verified property.
learn.realWorld: fit on training rows only and reuse the stored statistics at inference

learn.title: standardisation vs one-hot encoding
learn.body: standardisation means subtracting the training mean and dividing by the training standard deviation. one-hot encoding means representing each unordered category as its own binary column. They are easy to conflate, but confusing them changes which evidence a reviewer should ask for.
learn.realWorld: standardisation: converting features with different units into comparable z-scores

learn.title: standardisation: a design-review answer
learn.body: When asked how the team handles standardisation, answer with a mechanism and an artifact: fit on training rows only and reuse the stored statistics at inference. Then name the limitation: fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting. Intent alone is not an answer.
learn.realWorld: fit on training rows only and reuse the stored statistics at inference

learn.title: standardisation: a quick revision card

learn.title: standardisation: the interview trap

interview.q: Why must an imputer or scaler be fitted on training data only?
interview.answer: Fitting on all rows lets test-set statistics influence training, producing an optimistic estimate that will not reproduce in production. Fit on training data, then transform validation, test and live inputs with the same stored parameters.

interview.q: Why is one-hot encoding usually preferred over integer codes for unordered categories?
interview.answer: Integer codes imply an order and a distance: a model may treat “blue = 2” as twice “red = 1” and can interpolate a category that does not exist. One-hot encoding gives each category its own binary column, removing the false ordering at the cost of more columns.

coding.title: ml08 · cosine similarity · coding drill 1
coding.statement: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering: Compute the cosine similarity of 7, 6, 5 and 4, 3, 2. Write a complete Python snippet; the expected output is checked by the course test.
coding.starter:
import math
a = [7, 6, 5]
b = [4, 3, 2]
# calculate the requested value and print it to two decimals
coding.solution:
import math
a = [7, 6, 5]
b = [4, 3, 2]
answer = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b)) / (math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a)) * math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b)))
rounded = math.floor(answer * 100 + 0.5) / 100
print(f"{rounded:.2f}")
coding.hint: Divide the dot product by the product of both vector lengths.

coding.statement: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering: Compute the cosine similarity of 3, 2, 1 and 8, 7, 6. Write a complete Python snippet; the expected output is checked by the course test.
coding.starter:
import math
a = [3, 2, 1]
b = [8, 7, 6]
# calculate the requested value and print it to two decimals
coding.solution:
import math
a = [3, 2, 1]
b = [8, 7, 6]
answer = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b)) / (math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a)) * math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b)))
rounded = math.floor(answer * 100 + 0.5) / 100
print(f"{rounded:.2f}")
coding.hint: Divide the dot product by the product of both vector lengths.

logic.q: A one-hot encoder was fitted on red and green, then sees blue at inference. What should happen?
logic.answer: It should not silently map blue to red or green. A safe encoder is configured to ignore unknown categories, producing all zeros, or to reserve an explicit “unknown” column; the choice must match how the model was trained and be documented.

print([round(float(v), 2) for v in (x - x.mean()) / x.std()])

defense.q: How would you detect data leakage in a pipeline?
defense.answer: Compare suspiciously high validation scores with a simple baseline, trace every feature back to its timestamp, and check that all fitting happens inside a pipeline on training folds. A feature that would not exist at prediction time is leakage even if it improves the score.

defense.q: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering · Defend your approach to standardisation in a design review for Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering.
defense.answer: We treat standardisation as subtracting the training mean and dividing by the training standard deviation. The evidence is that we can fit on training rows only and reuse the stored statistics at inference. The limitation is that fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting

defense.q: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering · An interviewer challenges you: “fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting” How do you respond?
defense.answer: I would not defend the claim without evidence. I would show whether we can fit on training rows only and reuse the stored statistics at inference, and if we cannot, I would treat standardisation as an open risk rather than a solved property.

modules.title: ML Workflow and Model Fundamentals
modules.goal: Frame a problem, split honestly, establish a baseline, diagnose fit and run reproducible experiments.

topics.title: A chronological split for ordered data
topics.body: Rows are not always interchangeable. For time-ordered data, train on the past and test on the future; a random split can let the model learn from tomorrow to predict yesterday.
topics.code:
rows = list(range(10))
train, test = rows[:8], rows[8:]
print(len(train), len(test))

topics.title: A majority-class baseline
topics.body: Before any model, predict the most common class. This exposes imbalance and gives every later model a number it must beat on the same metric and split.
topics.code:
y = [1, 1, 0, 1]
print(round(max(y.count(0), y.count(1)) / len(y), 2))

topics.title: Overfitting, underfitting and cross-validation
topics.body: Underfitting misses the pattern in both training and validation. Overfitting captures noise, scoring high on training and lower on held-out data. K-fold cross-validation rotates the validation fold, giving a more stable estimate and a way to compare candidates without touching the test set.

interview.q: Why use stratified splitting for a classification problem?
interview.answer: Stratification preserves the class proportions in each split. With rare classes, a random split can leave almost none in validation or test, making the metric unstable or undefined. Stratify on the target when classes are imbalanced.

interview.q: What is data leakage, and what is one concrete example?
interview.answer: Data leakage is information from the target or the test period entering training, making validation look better than production. Scaling or imputing with statistics computed on the full dataset before the split is a common example; fit those steps on training data only.

coding.title: Majority baseline accuracy
coding.statement: For labels [0, 0, 1, 1, 1], print the accuracy of always predicting the majority class.
coding.starter:
labels = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1]
# print baseline
coding.solution:
labels = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1]
print(round(max(labels.count(0), labels.count(1)) / len(labels), 2))
coding.hint: Count the most frequent class, divide by all rows.

coding.title: Chronological split boundary
coding.statement: A dataset has 100 ordered rows and uses the first 80% for training. Print the number of training rows.
coding.starter:
rows = 100
train_fraction = 0.8
# print the boundary
coding.solution:
rows = 100
train_fraction = 0.8
print(int(rows * train_fraction))
coding.hint: The split is a position in the ordered rows, not a random sample.

debug.title: Tuning on the test set
debug.broken:
scores = [0.70, 0.75, 0.80]
best = max(scores)
print(f"test score: {best}")
debug.error: The maximum was selected using the test scores, so the reported test score is optimistically biased. Select with validation or cross-validation, then evaluate the chosen model once on test.
debug.fix:
validation = [0.70, 0.75, 0.80]
best = max(validation)
print(f"selected validation score: {best}")

defense.answer: Every look at the test set can influence later choices, turning it into a validation set and inflating the final estimate. Use validation or cross-validation for selection, then evaluate the final model once on test and report that result honestly.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: distinguish overfitting from underfitting and name one diagnostic for each.
checkpoint.answer: Overfitting fits training noise: training performance is much better than validation performance, often with high variance. Underfitting misses the real pattern: both training and validation performance are poor, often with high bias. Compare learning curves and training-versus-validation gaps; then simplify or regularise for overfitting, or add relevant capacity or features for underfitting.
rubric: Defines overfitting as a large train/validation gap.
Defines underfitting as poor performance on both training and validation.
Names a diagnostic and a corresponding response.
checkpoint.why: The two failures need opposite remedies; a single accuracy number cannot tell them apart.

logic.q: Training accuracy is 0.99 and validation accuracy is 0.60. Is the model overfitting or underfitting, and what should you check next?
logic.answer: It is overfitting: it fits the training rows far better than unseen rows. Check for leakage and an unrepresentative split, then simplify the model or add regularisation, more data or better validation before tuning further.

coding.title: Majority baseline accuracy

labels = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1]

defense.q: Why is the test set used only once?
defense.answer: Every look at the test set can influence later choices, turning it into a validation set and inflating the final estimate. Use validation or cross-validation for selection, then evaluate the final model once on test and report that result honestly.

defense.q: ML Workflow and Model Fundamentals · Defend your approach to baseline in a design review for ML Workflow and Model Fundamentals.
defense.answer: We treat baseline as the simplest defensible predictor a real model must beat. The evidence is that we can report the baseline and the candidate on the same split and metric. The limitation is that comparing a complex model only with another complex model

defense.q: ML Workflow and Model Fundamentals · An interviewer challenges you: “comparing a complex model only with another complex model” How do you respond?
defense.answer: I would not defend the claim without evidence. I would show whether we can report the baseline and the candidate on the same split and metric, and if we cannot, I would treat baseline as an open risk rather than a solved property.

defense.q: ML Workflow and Model Fundamentals · A production review asks for evidence on baseline. What do you show?
defense.answer: A reproducible check that report the baseline and the candidate on the same split and metric, the data and model version it used, and the failure it would catch: comparing a complex model only with another complex model.
steps: Tie it to the model version.

defense.q: ML Workflow and Model Fundamentals · What is the limitation of baseline, and how do you communicate it?
defense.answer: The limitation is that comparing a complex model only with another complex model. I would state it in the model card and pair it with the specific check “report the baseline and the candidate on the same split and metric” rather than implying the metric proves more than it does.
steps: Put it in the model card.

defense.q: ML Workflow and Model Fundamentals · If baseline fails after launch, what is your first response?
defense.answer: First contain the decision or alert path affected by the failure: comparing a complex model only with another complex model. modules.title: Linear Regression
modules.goal: Fit and interpret a linear model, calculate its errors and check the assumptions behind its coefficients.

topics.title: Fitting a line
topics.body: Simple linear regression chooses a slope and intercept that minimise squared error. `polyfit` with degree 1 is a compact way to see the fitted equation on a tiny dataset.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
y = np.array([2, 4, 6])
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
print(round(float(m), 1), round(float(b), 1))

topics.title: Mean squared error
topics.body: MSE averages the squared residuals. Squaring punishes large misses more than small ones, and the result is in squared target units; RMSE returns to the original unit.
topics.code:
y = [3, 5, 7]
p = [2, 5, 8]
print(round(sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(y, p)) / len(y), 2))

topics.title: R-squared, residuals and assumptions
topics.body: R² is the fraction of target variance explained relative to a mean baseline, but it can look high on a poor model and does not prove causation. Linear regression assumes a roughly linear relationship, independent errors, constant variance and no severe multicollinearity. Plot residuals; a pattern means the model is missing structure.

interview.q: What does R-squared not tell you?
interview.answer: It does not tell you whether the model is causally correct, whether predictions are useful at the decision threshold, or whether the assumptions hold. It can be inflated by adding features and can be low even when the model captures the business signal. Inspect residuals and use an error metric in target units.

interview.q: What does the intercept represent in a linear regression?
interview.answer: It is the prediction when every feature is zero. It anchors the line so the slope does not have to pass through the origin; in data where zero is outside the observed range, it is a mathematical anchor rather than a business-meaningful prediction.

coding.title: Recover a line’s slope
coding.statement: Fit a line to x = [1, 2, 3] and y = [3, 5, 7]; print the slope rounded to one decimal.
coding.starter:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
y = np.array([3, 5, 7])
# print slope
coding.solution:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
y = np.array([3, 5, 7])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
print(round(float(slope), 1))
coding.hint: Degree 1 returns slope first.

coding.title: Predict from a fitted line
coding.statement: For slope 2.5, intercept -1 and x = 4, print the prediction.
coding.starter:

logic.q: A model has R² = 0 on validation data. What does that mean relative to predicting the mean?
logic.answer: It means the model is no better than predicting the validation mean; R² compares the model’s squared error with that baseline. A negative R² means it is worse than the mean, which is possible on unseen data.

coding.title: Recover a line’s slope
coding.statement: Fit a line to x = [1, 2, 3] and y = [3, 5, 7]; print the slope rounded to one decimal.
coding.starter:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
y = np.array([3, 5, 7])
# print slope
coding.solution:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
y = np.array([3, 5, 7])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
print(round(float(slope), 1))
coding.hint: Degree 1 returns slope first.

coding.title: Predict from a fitted line
coding.statement: For slope 2.5, intercept -1 and x = 4, print the prediction.
coding.starter:
slope = 2.5
intercept = -1
x = 4
# print the prediction
coding.solution:
slope = 2.5
intercept = -1
x = 4
print(slope * x + intercept)
coding.hint: Multiply the input by the slope, then add the intercept.

coding.title: ml10 · mean squared error · coding drill 1
coding.statement: Linear Regression: Actual values are 2, 9, 16, 3 and predictions are 10, 17, 4, 11. What is the MSE, rounded to two decimals? Write a complete Python snippet; the expected output is checked by the course test.
coding.starter:
import math
actual = [2, 9, 16, 3]
predicted = [10, 17, 4, 11]
# calculate the requested value and print it to two decimals
coding.solution:
import math
actual = [2, 9, 16, 3]
predicted = [10, 17, 4, 11]
answer = sum((a - p) ** 2 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted)) / len(actual)
rounded = math.floor(answer * 100 + 0.5) / 100
print(f"{rounded:.2f}")
coding.hint: Square each residual, add, then divide by the number of rows.

logic.q: A model has R² = 0 on validation data. What does that mean relative to predicting the mean?
logic.answer: It means the model is no better than predicting the validation mean; R² compares the model’s squared error with that baseline. A negative R² means it is worse than the mean, which is possible on unseen data.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Fitting a line
practice.task: Simple linear regression chooses a slope and intercept that minimise squared error. `polyfit` with degree 1 is a compact way to see the fitted equation on a tiny dataset.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])

print(round(float(m), 1), round(float(b), 1))

defense.answer: R² measures explained variance on one sample, not the decision cost, calibration, fairness or stability in production. A model can explain variance overall while being systematically wrong for a subgroup or unusable when inputs drift.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: interpret a regression slope and intercept, and state one thing R-squared does not tell you.
checkpoint.answer: The slope is the predicted change in the target for a one-unit increase in the feature, holding the model fixed. The intercept is the prediction when the feature is zero, which may be outside the observed range. R-squared describes the share of variance explained in this sample; it does not prove causation or guarantee good predictions on a different population.
checkpoint.why: The slope is conditional on the model and feature scale; R-squared is an in-sample fit summary, not a causal or deployment guarantee.
