coding.title: Cosine similarity of two vectors
coding.statement: For a = [2, 0] and b = [1, 1], print cosine similarity rounded to two decimals.
coding.starter:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 0])
b = np.array([1, 1])
# similarity
coding.solution:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 0])
b = np.array([1, 1])
print(round(float(a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))), 2))
coding.hint: Dot product over the product of norms.

coding.title: ml22 · cosine similarity · coding drill 1
coding.statement: Recommendation Systems: Compute the cosine similarity of 5, 4, 3 and 2, 1, 8. Write a complete Python snippet; the expected output is checked by the course test.
coding.starter:
import math
a = [5, 4, 3]
b = [2, 1, 8]
# calculate the requested value and print it to two decimals
coding.solution:
import math
a = [5, 4, 3]
b = [2, 1, 8]
answer = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b)) / (math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a)) * math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b)))
rounded = math.floor(answer * 100 + 0.5) / 100
print(f"{rounded:.2f}")
coding.hint: Divide the dot product by the product of both vector lengths.

logic.q: What is the cosine similarity of the vectors [1, 0] and [0, 1], and what does it mean for recommendations?
logic.answer: It is 0. The vectors are orthogonal, so they share no direction; cosine similarity measures angle rather than magnitude, and a zero score means no similarity in that feature space.

print(round(float(a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))), 2))

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Cosine similarity
practice.task: Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors, ignoring magnitude. It is common for user-item behaviour because a user who interacts more should not automatically be “more similar” to everything.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 0])
b = np.array([1, 1])
print(round(float(a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))), 2))

defense.q: Why is offline rating accuracy a weak recommender metric?
defense.answer: A recommender’s job is to rank a short list that changes behaviour, not to predict every rating perfectly. Rating RMSE can improve while the top items are boring or already seen. Evaluate ranking with precision@k, recall@k, NDCG and online outcomes such as clicks or conversions.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain the cold-start problem and one way content features can reduce it.
checkpoint.answer: Cold start is the lack of interaction history for a new user or item, so collaborative filtering has no ratings to compare. Content features such as genre, description or user-declared interests can place the new entity near known ones and provide an initial recommendation. As interactions arrive, the system can blend or switch to collaborative signals.
checkpoint.why: Cold start is an information problem; content features provide a prior until behavioural data exists.

modules.title: Natural Language Processing with Classical ML
modules.goal: Turn text into features, classify sentiment and evaluate a text pipeline without leaking the vocabulary.

topics.title: Token frequency with Counter
topics.body: A bag-of-words representation counts tokens and ignores order. Counter is a compact way to see the vocabulary and frequencies before vectorising.
topics.code:
from collections import Counter
print(dict(Counter("a b a".split())))

topics.title: A TF-IDF score
topics.body: TF-IDF raises the weight of a term that is frequent in a document but rare across documents. Here term frequency 0.2 times inverse document frequency 2 gives 0.4.
topics.code:
tf, idf = 0.2, 2
print(round(tf * idf, 2))

topics.title: Cleaning, stemming and evaluation
topics.body: Text cleaning removes markup, normalises case and handles punctuation. Tokenisation splits text; stopword removal drops very common words; stemming cuts suffixes aggressively while lemmatisation uses a dictionary and part of speech. Fit the vectoriser on training text only. Evaluate with precision, recall and F1 per class, and inspect misclassified examples for sarcasm, negation and domain language.

interview.q: What is the difference between stemming and lemmatisation?
interview.answer: Stemming applies crude suffix rules and may produce non-words (“studies” → “studi”). Lemmatisation maps a word to a valid dictionary form using linguistic information (“studies” → “study”). Lemmatisation is slower but more interpretable; stemming is a fast baseline.

interview.q: Why is TF-IDF often better than raw word counts for text classification?
interview.answer: TF-IDF downweights terms that appear in many documents, so common words such as “the” do not dominate, while terms frequent in one document but rare across the corpus receive more weight. It still produces a sparse, high-dimensional representation and does not understand word order or meaning.

coding.title: Count word frequencies

debug.title: Fitting the vectoriser on all text
debug.broken:
texts = ["good movie", "bad movie"]
vocabulary = set(" ".join(texts).split())
print(sorted(vocabulary))
debug.error: The vocabulary was built from every document, including the test documents. That leaks test vocabulary into training. Fit the vectoriser on the training split only, then transform held-out text with the same vocabulary.
debug.fix:
train = ["good movie"]
vocabulary = set(" ".join(train).split())
print(sorted(vocabulary))

defense.answer: Class imbalance and easy neutral examples can dominate accuracy while the model fails on negations, sarcasm or a minority class. checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain TF-IDF and why it often helps text classification.
checkpoint.answer: TF-IDF multiplies a term’s frequency in a document by a weight that falls as the term appears in more documents. Common words such as “the” are downweighted, while terms that distinguish a document are emphasised. It produces a sparse, interpretable feature vector, though it ignores word order and deeper meaning.
rubric: Explains term frequency and inverse document frequency.
States that common terms are downweighted and discriminative terms emphasised.
Names a limitation such as sparsity, no word order or no semantics.
checkpoint.why: The IDF factor turns raw counts into a relative signal; it is still a bag-of-words representation.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (true/false): TF-IDF generally downweights terms that appear in many documents.
options: True
False
checkpoint.answer: True
checkpoint.why: The inverse-document-frequency factor falls as a term becomes more common across the corpus, reducing the weight of ubiquitous words.

checkpoint.answer: lower
checkpoint.why: Lowercasing makes “ML” and “ml” the same token before splitting, deduplicating and sorting.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why a text vectoriser must be fitted on training text only.
checkpoint.answer: The vectoriser learns a vocabulary and document frequencies from the text it sees. Fitting on all rows lets test or future text influence the feature space, which is leakage and produces an optimistic estimate. Fit on training text, then transform validation, test and live text with the stored vocabulary; handle unseen terms explicitly.
rubric: Names vocabulary or document-frequency statistics as learned state.
Explains how all-data fitting leaks evaluation information.
Requires fitting on training text and transforming later data with the stored state.
checkpoint.why: The feature representation is part of the model; learning it from the evaluation set contaminates the comparison.

logic.q: A document has the tokens ["cat", "cat", "dog"]. What is the term frequency of "cat" within the document?
logic.answer: It is 2/3, or about 0.67. Term frequency is the count of the term divided by the total number of tokens in that document; document frequency, which TF-IDF also uses, counts how many documents contain it.

learn.title: tokenisation: the working definition
learn.body: tokenisation means splitting text into the units a model will represent. In Natural Language Processing with Classical ML, the practical test is whether that definition changes a decision rather than merely appearing in a notebook. Example: splitting “ML is fun” into three lowercase tokens.

learn.title: tokenisation: why it changes decisions
learn.body: A team can produce a polished model and still get tokenisation wrong. The failure looks like this: removing negation during cleaning and reversing sentiment. The countermeasure is to inspect tokens on examples where meaning would flip and to name the evidence in the design review.

interview.q: What is the difference between stemming and lemmatisation?
interview.answer: Stemming applies crude suffix rules and may produce non-words (“studies” → “studi”). Lemmatisation maps a word to a valid dictionary form using linguistic information (“studies” → “study”). Lemmatisation is slower but more interpretable; stemming is a fast baseline.

interview.q: Why is TF-IDF often better than raw word counts for text classification?
interview.answer: TF-IDF downweights terms that appear in many documents, so common words such as “the” do not dominate, while terms frequent in one document but rare across the corpus receive more weight. It still produces a sparse, high-dimensional representation and does not understand word order or meaning.

weights = [2, 4, 1]

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain TF-IDF and why it often helps text classification.
checkpoint.answer: TF-IDF multiplies a term’s frequency in a document by a weight that falls as the term appears in more documents. Common words such as “the” are downweighted, while terms that distinguish a document are emphasised. It produces a sparse, interpretable feature vector, though it ignores word order and deeper meaning.
checkpoint.why: The IDF factor turns raw counts into a relative signal; it is still a bag-of-words representation.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (true/false): TF-IDF generally downweights terms that appear in many documents.
checkpoint.answer: True
options: True
False
checkpoint.why: The inverse-document-frequency factor falls as a term becomes more common across the corpus, reducing the weight of ubiquitous words.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why a text vectoriser must be fitted on training text only.
checkpoint.answer: The vectoriser learns a vocabulary and document frequencies from the text it sees. Fitting on all rows lets test or future text influence the feature space, which is leakage and produces an optimistic estimate. Fit on training text, then transform validation, test and live text with the stored vocabulary; handle unseen terms explicitly.
checkpoint.why: The feature representation is part of the model; learning it from the evaluation set contaminates the comparison.

modules.title: Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML
modules.goal: See how a neuron, activation and backpropagation connect classical ML to deep learning and modern AI.

topics.title: A single perceptron step
topics.body: A perceptron computes a weighted sum and applies a step function. Here weights [1, -1] on inputs [1, 1] give 0, so the step output is 0. The bias would shift the threshold.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 1])
w = np.array([1, -1])
print(int((w @ x) > 0))

topics.title: A ReLU-like activation
topics.body: An activation introduces non-linearity. Without it, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear transformation. This compares each value with zero to produce [0, 0, 1].
topics.code:
z = [-1, 0, 1]
print([int(v > 0) for v in z])

topics.title: Backpropagation, embeddings and transformers
topics.body: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute each weight’s gradient, then an optimiser updates the weights. Embeddings learn dense vectors for categories or tokens. Transformers use attention to weigh context, which is why they power modern language models. Traditional ML remains the right first choice for many tabular problems; this module is a bridge to the separate BroCode Deep Learning course.

interview.q: Why is an activation function necessary in a neural network?
interview.answer: Without a non-linear activation, any stack of linear layers is equivalent to a single linear layer, no matter how deep. Activations let the network represent curved boundaries and complex interactions. ReLU, sigmoid and tanh are common choices with different gradient behaviour.

interview.q: What does backpropagation compute, and what does the optimiser do with it?
interview.answer: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. The optimiser uses those gradients to update the weights, for example with gradient descent or Adam; backpropagation computes direction, the optimiser decides the step.

coding.title: Perceptron output
coding.statement: For inputs [1, 1], weights [1, -1] and threshold 0, print 1 if the weighted sum is positive, else 0.

coding.solution:
x = [1, 1]
w = [1, -1]
score = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(x, w))
print(int(score > 0))
coding.hint: Compute the weighted sum first.

coding.title: Dense layer parameter count
coding.statement: A dense layer has 3 inputs and 2 outputs and uses a bias for each output. Print the total number of trainable parameters.
coding.starter:

outputs = 2
# print the parameter count
coding.solution:
inputs = 3
outputs = 2
print((inputs + 1) * outputs)
coding.hint: Each output has one weight per input plus one bias.

debug.title: Stacking linear layers without activation
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.0])
W1, W2 = np.array([[2.0]]), np.array([[3.0]])
print(W2 @ W1 @ x)
debug.error: The output is 6x, which is just one linear layer 6x. Without an activation between W1 and W2, depth adds no representational power. Insert a non-linear activation.
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.0])
W1, W2 = np.array([[2.0]]), np.array([[3.0]])
hidden = np.maximum(0, W1 @ x)
print(W2 @ hidden)

defense.q: When would you choose a classical ML model over a neural network?
defense.answer: Choose classical ML for small or medium tabular datasets, strict interpretability, limited compute, fast iteration or a strong baseline requirement. Neural networks dominate images, audio and language where representation learning matters and data is plentiful. The best choice is empirical and cost-aware, not a status symbol.

learn.title: perceptron: the working definition
learn.body: perceptron means a weighted sum followed by a step or threshold activation. In Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML, the practical test is whether that definition changes a decision rather than merely appearing in a notebook. Example: weights [1, -1] on inputs [1, 1] producing a zero score.
learn.realWorld: weights [1, -1] on inputs [1, 1] producing a zero score

learn.title: perceptron: why it changes decisions
learn.body: A team can produce a polished model and still get perceptron wrong. The failure looks like this: assuming one perceptron can solve a non-linear boundary. The countermeasure is to test the boundary on a small non-linear fixture and to name the evidence in the design review.
learn.realWorld: test the boundary on a small non-linear fixture

learn.title: perceptron: a worked example

learn.realWorld: weights [1, -1] on inputs [1, 1] producing a zero score

learn.title: perceptron: the failure mode

learn.realWorld: assuming one perceptron can solve a non-linear boundary

interview.q: Why is an activation function necessary in a neural network?
interview.answer: Without a non-linear activation, any stack of linear layers is equivalent to a single linear layer, no matter how deep. Activations let the network represent curved boundaries and complex interactions. ReLU, sigmoid and tanh are common choices with different gradient behaviour.

interview.q: What does backpropagation compute, and what does the optimiser do with it?
interview.answer: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. The optimiser uses those gradients to update the weights, for example with gradient descent or Adam; backpropagation computes direction, the optimiser decides the step.

coding.title: Perceptron output
coding.statement: For inputs [1, 1], weights [1, -1] and threshold 0, print 1 if the weighted sum is positive, else 0.
coding.starter:
x = [1, 1]
w = [1, -1]
# perceptron
coding.solution:
x = [1, 1]
w = [1, -1]
score = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(x, w))
print(int(score > 0))
coding.hint: Compute the weighted sum first.

outputs = 2

coding.title: ml24 · dot product · coding drill 1
coding.statement: Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML: Compute the dot product of 8, 6, 4 and 2, 9, 7. Write a complete Python snippet; the expected output is checked by the course test.
coding.starter:
import math
a = [8, 6, 4]
b = [2, 9, 7]
# calculate the requested value and print it to two decimals
coding.solution:
import math
a = [8, 6, 4]
b = [2, 9, 7]
answer = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
rounded = math.floor(answer * 100 + 0.5) / 100
print(f"{rounded:.2f}")
coding.hint: Multiply matching positions, then add the products.

coding.title: ml24 · sigmoid · coding drill 1
coding.statement: Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML: What is the sigmoid of z = -4, rounded to two decimals? Write a complete Python snippet; the expected output is checked by the course test.
coding.starter:
import math
z = -4
# calculate the requested value and print it to two decimals
coding.solution:
import math
z = -4
answer = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))
rounded = math.floor(answer * 100 + 0.5) / 100
print(f"{rounded:.2f}")
coding.hint: The sigmoid is 1 / (1 + e^-z).

coding.title: ml24 · gradient descent step · coding drill 1
coding.statement: Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML: A weight is 10, its gradient is 4 and the learning rate is 0.1. What is the next weight, rounded to two decimals? Write a complete Python snippet; the expected output is checked by the course test.
coding.starter:
import math
weight = 10
gradient = 4
lr = 0.1
# calculate the requested value and print it to two decimals
coding.solution:
import math
weight = 10
gradient = 4
lr = 0.1
answer = weight - lr * gradient
rounded = math.floor(answer * 100 + 0.5) / 100
print(f"{rounded:.2f}")
coding.hint: Move opposite the gradient: weight minus learning rate times gradient.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: A single perceptron step
practice.task: A perceptron computes a weighted sum and applies a step function. Here weights [1, -1] on inputs [1, 1] give 0, so the step output is 0. The bias would shift the threshold.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 1])
w = np.array([1, -1])
print(int((w @ x) > 0))

defense.q: When would you choose a classical ML model over a neural network?
defense.answer: Choose classical ML for small or medium tabular datasets, strict interpretability, limited compute, fast iteration or a strong baseline requirement. Neural networks dominate images, audio and language where representation learning matters and data is plentiful. The best choice is empirical and cost-aware, not a status symbol.

defense.q: Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML · Defend your approach to perceptron in a design review for Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML.
defense.answer: We treat perceptron as a weighted sum followed by a step or threshold activation. The evidence is that we can test the boundary on a small non-linear fixture. The limitation is that assuming one perceptron can solve a non-linear boundary

defense.q: Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML · An interviewer challenges you: “assuming one perceptron can solve a non-linear boundary” How do you respond?
defense.answer: I would not defend the claim without evidence. I would show whether we can test the boundary on a small non-linear fixture, and if we cannot, I would treat perceptron as an open risk rather than a solved property.

defense.q: Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML · A production review asks for evidence on perceptron. What do you show?
defense.answer: A reproducible check that test the boundary on a small non-linear fixture, the data and model version it used, and the failure it would catch: assuming one perceptron can solve a non-linear boundary.
steps: Tie it to the model version.

defense.q: Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML · What is the limitation of perceptron, and how do you communicate it?
defense.answer: The limitation is that assuming one perceptron can solve a non-linear boundary. I would state it in the model card and pair it with the specific check “test the boundary on a small non-linear fixture” rather than implying the metric proves more than it does.
steps: Put it in the model card.

defense.q: Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML · If perceptron fails after launch, what is your first response?
defense.answer: First contain the decision or alert path affected by the failure: assuming one perceptron can solve a non-linear boundary. Then reproduce the check “test the boundary on a small non-linear fixture”, quantify the scope, and decide whether to roll back or add a guardrail.
steps: Roll back or add a guardrail.

defense.q: Introduction to Neural Networks and Modern ML · How would you teach perceptron to a new teammate without oversimplifying it?
defense.answer: Start with the definition—a weighted sum followed by a step or threshold activation—then walk through the example: weights [1, -1] on inputs [1, 1] producing a zero score. End with the failure and its check: assuming one perceptron can solve a non-linear boundary and test the boundary on a small non-linear fixture.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain why activation functions are necessary and what backpropagation computes.
checkpoint.answer: Without a non-linear activation, stacked layers compose into one linear transformation, so depth adds no representational power. A non-linearity lets the network learn curved decision boundaries and complex features. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute the loss gradient with respect to every weight; the optimiser then uses those gradients to update the weights.
checkpoint.why: Activation changes the function class; backpropagation changes how parameters are learned, not the network’s forward capacity.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain what backpropagation computes and what the optimiser does with it.

modules.title: ML Pipelines, Engineering and Testing
modules.goal: Package preprocessing and models into reproducible, testable pipelines that behave the same in training and production.

topics.title: Function composition
topics.body: A pipeline is composition: the output of one step becomes the input of the next. This tiny example gives 7 because double(3) is 6 and add_one(6) is 7.

topics.title: Apply training statistics at inference
topics.body: A fitted transformation stores its training statistics. At inference, the same numbers are applied to a new value; recomputing the mean on live data would change the transformation and break train/serve consistency.
topics.code:
train_mean, live_value = 2.0, 4.0
print(round(live_value - train_mean, 2))

topics.title: Serialization, testing and train/serve skew
topics.body: A pipeline object should own imputation, encoding, scaling and the estimator so one `.fit` and one `.predict` reproduce the whole path. Joblib is common for scikit-learn artifacts; pickle can execute code, so never load untrusted files. Test schema, missing columns, unseen categories, numeric ranges and a known prediction. Train/serve skew is when production preprocessing differs from training preprocessing.

interview.q: What is train/serve skew and how do you prevent it?
interview.answer: It is any difference between the features a model saw in training and the features it receives in production: different units, fill values, category mappings or time windows. Prevent it by sharing one preprocessing pipeline, validating input schemas, logging the exact feature vector and comparing offline and online distributions.

interview.q: What is the difference between a transformer and an estimator in scikit-learn?
interview.answer: A transformer learns a feature transformation, typically with `fit` and `transform`, such as scaling or imputation. An estimator learns to predict a target with `fit` and `predict`. A Pipeline chains transformers into a final estimator so the same fitted preprocessing is used in training and inference.

coding.title: Compose two steps
coding.statement: Apply double then add_one to 5 and print the result.
coding.hint: Order matters: double first, then add one.

coding.title: Apply the training mean
coding.statement: Training values are [1, 3]. Print the transformed value of a test value 5 after subtracting the training mean.
coding.starter:
train = [1, 3]
test_value = 5
# apply the training mean
coding.solution:
train = [1, 3]
test_value = 5
print(test_value - sum(train) / len(train))
coding.hint: Compute the mean on training rows only, then reuse that number.

debug.title: Fitting the pipeline on live data
debug.broken:
train_mean = 2.0
live_mean = 4.0
value = 6.0
print(value - live_mean)
debug.error: The transformation uses the live mean instead of the stored training mean, so the model receives a feature on a different scale. Store the training statistic in the pipeline and reuse it, never refit on each request.
debug.fix:
train_mean = 2.0
value = 6.0
print(value - train_mean)

mini.title: A reusable preprocessing pipeline
mini.brief: Package imputation, scaling and a model into one object and test it on a held-out row.
steps: Fit the pipeline on training rows.
Assert the output shape and range.

lab.title: Production-shaped pipeline package
lab.brief: Create a small Python package with a fitted pipeline artifact, schema validation and tests.
milestones: Test a known prediction after reload.

defense.q: Why is a pickled model without its preprocessing incomplete?
defense.answer: The estimator expects features in the exact representation used during fitting. A naked model plus a separately reimplemented scaler is a train/serve skew risk. Serialize the whole pipeline and its schema, then version them together.
steps: Save the pipeline, not just the estimator.

checkpoint.q: A scikit-learn Pipeline helps prevent:
options: Preprocessing leakage and train/serve skew
All model bias
The need for tests
checkpoint.answer: Preprocessing leakage and train/serve skew
checkpoint.why: One object fits and applies every step consistently.

checkpoint.q: Pickle should be loaded only from:
options: Trusted sources
Any public download
An email attachment
checkpoint.answer: Trusted sources
checkpoint.why: Unpickling can execute arbitrary code.

checkpoint.q: True or false: fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting is safe because scaling is unsupervised.
options: True
False
checkpoint.answer: False
checkpoint.why: Unsupervised does not mean leakage-free. The scaler learns the test set’s mean and spread, so evaluation information influences training preprocessing.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain train/serve skew and one pipeline practice that prevents it.
checkpoint.answer: Train/serve skew is when training and inference apply different preprocessing, feature order, defaults or model versions, so production inputs do not match what the model learned. Package preprocessing and the estimator in one pipeline, fit it once on training data, and reuse the same artifact and schema at inference. Log the feature contract and test a real request path.

logic.q: A scaler is fitted on all rows before the train/test split. Why is the resulting validation score optimistic?
logic.answer: The scaler has already seen the test rows’ mean and spread, so information from the evaluation set influenced training. That is preprocessing leakage; fit the scaler inside the training fold or pipeline, then transform the held-out data with those training statistics.

interview.q: What is train/serve skew and how do you prevent it?
interview.answer: It is any difference between the features a model saw in training and the features it receives in production: different units, fill values, category mappings or time windows. Prevent it by sharing one preprocessing pipeline, validating input schemas, logging the exact feature vector and comparing offline and online distributions.

interview.q: What is the difference between a transformer and an estimator in scikit-learn?
interview.answer: A transformer learns a feature transformation, typically with `fit` and `transform`, such as scaling or imputation. An estimator learns to predict a target with `fit` and `predict`. A Pipeline chains transformers into a final estimator so the same fitted preprocessing is used in training and inference.

logic.q: A scaler is fitted on all rows before the train/test split. Why is the resulting validation score optimistic?

defense.q: Why is a pickled model without its preprocessing incomplete?
defense.answer: The estimator expects features in the exact representation used during fitting. A naked model plus a separately reimplemented scaler is a train/serve skew risk. Serialize the whole pipeline and its schema, then version them together.
steps: Save the pipeline, not just the estimator.

defense.q: ML Pipelines, Engineering and Testing · Defend your approach to pipeline in a design review for ML Pipelines, Engineering and Testing.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (fill in the blank): restore the missing token in this Function composition sample.
checkpoint.why: The missing token is 3; with it restored the sample prints 7. A pipeline is composition: the output of one step becomes the input of the next. This tiny example gives 7 because double(3) is 6 and add_one(6) is 7.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (code output): predict exactly what this Apply training statistics at inference sample prints.
checkpoint.code:
train_mean, live_value = 2.0, 4.0
print(round(live_value - train_mean, 2))
checkpoint.why: The verified output is 2.0. A fitted transformation stores its training statistics. At inference, the same numbers are applied to a new value; recomputing the mean on live data would change the transformation and break train/serve consistency.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain train/serve skew and one pipeline practice that prevents it.
checkpoint.answer: Train/serve skew is when training and inference apply different preprocessing, feature order, defaults or model versions, so production inputs do not match what the model learned. Package preprocessing and the estimator in one pipeline, fit it once on training data, and reuse the same artifact and schema at inference. Log the feature contract and test a real request path.
checkpoint.why: The model only sees the features serving produces; a correct model with different preprocessing is still wrong.
rubric: Defines skew as a difference between training and serving transformations or contracts.
Recommends one shared fitted pipeline or artifact rather than duplicated code.
Mentions validation of the actual serving path, schema or version.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (true/false): a preprocessing pipeline should be fitted separately on the training and test sets.
checkpoint.answer: False
options: True
False
checkpoint.why: Fit once on training data, then transform validation, test and serving data with the same stored object. Separate fitting leaks test statistics and creates inconsistency.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (fill in the blank): restore the training mean in this inference calculation.
checkpoint.answer: mean
checkpoint.code:
train = [1, 3]
test_value = 5
mean = sum(train) / len(train)
print(test_value - ___)
checkpoint.solution:
train = [1, 3]
test_value = 5
mean = sum(train) / len(train)
print(test_value - mean)
checkpoint.why: The training mean is 2.0; applying it to the test value 5 gives 3.0 without recomputing from test data.

Package preprocessing and the estimator in one fitted pipeline, version the artifact and schema, and test the real serving path with a known fixture.
checkpoint.why: A correct model fed differently transformed features is still wrong in production.

modules.title: Model Deployment and MLOps
modules.goal: Serve a model behind a validated API, containerise it, monitor drift and close the retraining loop.

topics.title: Validate an input payload
topics.body: An API must reject malformed input before it reaches the model. Checking that a required field exists and is positive is a minimal contract; real services also validate types, ranges and unknown fields.
topics.code:
payload = {"age": 30}
print("age" in payload and payload["age"] > 0)

topics.title: A health response
topics.body: A health endpoint reports whether the service can serve traffic. It should be cheap and must not expose secrets or model internals. This dictionary is the shape a client can check.
topics.code:
status = {"status": "ok"}
print(status["status"])

topics.title: Docker, experiment tracking and drift
topics.body: Docker packages the API, dependencies and model artifact into a reproducible image; environment variables supply configuration without baking secrets into the image. MLflow tracks runs, parameters and artifacts and can host a model registry; DVC versions data and large artifacts alongside Git. In production, monitor input drift, prediction drift and delayed outcomes, then retrain only through a tested, versioned workflow.

coding.starter:
import math
tp = 19
fp = 7
fn = 14
# calculate the requested value and print it to two decimals
coding.solution:
import math
tp = 19
fp = 7
fn = 14
answer = 2 * (tp / (tp + fp)) * (tp / (tp + fn)) / ((tp / (tp + fp)) + (tp / (tp + fn)))
rounded = math.floor(answer * 100 + 0.5) / 100
print(f"{rounded:.2f}")
coding.hint: F1 is 2 × precision × recall divided by precision + recall.

logic.q: A health endpoint returns 200, but the model file it needs is missing. Is the service ready to serve predictions?
logic.answer: No. A liveness check can say the process is running, but readiness must verify the model artifact and dependencies. Return a failure from readiness and keep the service out of traffic until it can actually serve; a 200 that hides a missing model is a false health signal.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain the difference between liveness and readiness, and why a model version should be recorded.
checkpoint.answer: Liveness says the process is running; readiness says it can actually serve traffic, including a loaded model and available dependencies. A 200 from a liveness endpoint does not prove the model artifact is present. Recording the model version and preprocessing version makes predictions reproducible, supports rollback and lets you investigate drift or incidents.
checkpoint.why: A live process can still be unable to predict; readiness and artifact provenance are separate operational guarantees.

interview.q: What are the limits of explainability?
interview.answer: An explanation describes the model’s behaviour, not the causal effect of a feature or the correctness of the data. Correlated features can share credit arbitrarily, local explanations can disagree with global ones, and a plausible explanation can still justify a harmful decision. interview.q: What is the difference between fairness through unawareness and measuring disparate impact?

logic.q: A model has equal accuracy for groups A and B, but it approves group A at twice the rate. Does equal accuracy prove the model is fair?
logic.answer: No. Equal accuracy can coexist with very different selection rates, error types or false-positive costs. Fairness depends on the decision and the harm; report outcome rates, error rates by group and sample sizes before making a claim.

import math
tp = 9
fn = 12
answer = tp / (tp + fn)

print(f"{rounded:.2f}")

checkpoint.q: A fairness audit should report:
checkpoint.answer: Metrics by relevant subgroup with sample sizes
options: Metrics by relevant subgroup with sample sizes
Only the overall average
Only the model file size
checkpoint.why: Aggregate metrics can hide group-level harm.

checkpoint.q: A capstone is strongest when it includes:
checkpoint.answer: A reproducible run and documented limitations
options: A reproducible run and documented limitations
Only a screenshot of a high score
A hidden dataset
checkpoint.why: Evidence and honest limits are what an interviewer can evaluate.

checkpoint.q: True or false: equal accuracy across two groups proves that the model approves both groups at equal rates.
checkpoint.answer: False
options: True
False
checkpoint.why: Accuracy and selection rate are different metrics. A model can be equally accurate while approving one group much more often, or vice versa.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (fill in the blank): restore the missing token in this A demographic parity gap sample.
checkpoint.code:
a, b = ___ / 100, 40 / 100
print(round(abs(a - b), 2))
checkpoint.solution:
a, b = 60 / 100, 40 / 100
print(round(abs(a - b), 2))
checkpoint.why: The missing token is 60; with it restored the sample prints 0.2. A fairness audit compares a metric across groups. Here one group’s positive rate is 0.6 and another’s is 0.4; the absolute gap is 0.2. This gap is a diagnostic, not a complete fairness verdict.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (code output): predict exactly what this An accuracy gap across groups sample prints.
checkpoint.code:
a, b = 0.9, 0.6
print(round(a - b, 2))
checkpoint.why: The verified output is 0.3. Overall accuracy can hide a group that the model serves badly. Reporting 0.9 for one group and 0.6 for another exposes a 0.3 gap that an aggregate score would obscure.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: explain the difference between demographic parity and equal accuracy, and why fairness still needs context.
checkpoint.answer: Demographic parity compares selection or positive-decision rates across groups; equal accuracy compares overall correctness within each group. A model can have equal accuracy while approving one group at a much higher rate, or equal rates while making different kinds of errors. The appropriate fairness question depends on the decision, the harm and the affected population, so multiple group-level metrics and context are needed.
checkpoint.why: Parity and accuracy measure different things; neither alone establishes fair treatment.
rubric: Defines demographic parity as comparable selection or positive rates.
Defines equal accuracy as comparable correctness, and notes that the two can diverge.
States that fairness depends on context, harms or the decision, not one universal metric.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (true/false): equal accuracy across two groups proves that the model approves both groups at equal rates.
checkpoint.answer: False
options: True
False
checkpoint.why: Accuracy and positive-decision rate are different metrics. A model can be equally accurate while selecting one group much more often.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint (fill in the blank): restore the larger rate in this disparate-impact ratio.
checkpoint.answer: max(rate_a, rate_b)
checkpoint.code:
rate_a = 0.6
rate_b = 0.3
print(round(min(rate_a, rate_b) / ___, 2))
checkpoint.solution:
rate_a = 0.6
rate_b = 0.3
print(round(min(rate_a, rate_b) / max(rate_a, rate_b), 2))
checkpoint.why: The disparate-impact ratio divides the lower rate by the higher one: 0.3 / 0.6 = 0.5.

checkpoint.q: Written checkpoint: an audit finds equal accuracy but different approval rates. Explain which fairness question is unanswered and what evidence you need.
checkpoint.answer: Demographic parity compares positive or selection rates across groups; equal accuracy compares correctness within each group. A model can have equal accuracy while approving one group much more often, or equal rates while making different kinds of errors. The appropriate fairness question depends on the decision, the harm and the affected population, so report several group-level metrics and the context.
checkpoint.why: Parity and accuracy measure different things; neither alone establishes fair treatment.
rubric: Defines demographic parity as comparable selection or positive rates.
Defines equal accuracy as comparable correctness and notes they can diverge.
States that fairness depends on context, harms or the decision.
